independent.summary: Rule 5 requires a string `code`, but body-parser's errors (`entity.parse.failed`, `entity.too.large`) carry only `status`/`statusCode`/`type` — so a malformed JSON body or an over-100kB body on any endpoint except `/import` now falls to rule 6 and answers 500 `INTERNAL` where Express's finalhandler previously honoured the 400/413. `src/routes/import.js:63` states this outright ('a `SyntaxError` answered as the caller's 400 instead of falling through to the error handler's 500'), so every other router now reports a client mistake as a server fault, with a `ref` and a logged stack per bad request.

`draft.diagnostics.error = err.message` persists the raw generation error, and `GET /drafts/:id` (line 730) returns the whole lean document — so the driver's/provider's verbatim text (a Mongo pool error from a grounding read included) still reaches a caller in a plain JSON response body, contradicting docs/api.md's 'the driver's own text never reaches a caller'. The source sweep cannot see it because the leak is a stored field, not an `err.message` in a `res.json(...)` statement, and SSE scoping does not cover this non-SSE route.

The falsification note claims that dropping `app.use(errorHandler)` from `src/app.js` makes 'the first three groups' fail, but the duplicate-key, explicit-code, cast and opaque groups all run against `buildProbeApp()`, which mounts `errorHandler` itself — only the schema-validation group exercises the real app's mount, so three of the four stated defences would still pass with the production mount removed.

The Errors section documents `httpError(503, 'EXPORT_NOT_CONFIGURED')` as how a route raises a coded refusal and lists `INVALID_ID`, `INVALID_WORKSPACE_NAME`, `NOT_WORKSPACE_*` and `EXPORT_NOT_CONFIGURED` as the codes 'in use' through that path, but no file under `server/src/` calls `httpError` (only the test does) and every one of those codes is a direct `res.status(...).json(...)` that never reaches rule 5 — the documented mechanism has no production caller.

The handler's first branch is exactly `if (res.headersSent)`, and delegating to Express there is correct — no body can be written over a started response, so `next(err)` closing the socket is the intended ending, not a defect.
